Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for six long years the government has taken a meat cleaver to Canada's national institutions. It has slashed and hacked away indiscriminately at passenger rail service, health care services, old age pensions, Air Canada, youth employment programs, and the unemployment insurance program. Now it is the CBC that is on the chopping block.
Canadians are learning today that the CBC is closing as many as 10 of its regional TV stations, including a station in Sydney, Nova Scotia, that serves my entire riding, and a French language station outside Quebec, both of which are building blocks of national unity. As many as 2,000 jobs may be cut.
Surely the federal government has a duty and an obligation to enhance the quality of Canadian life and not a licence to dismantle those institutions that bind Canadians together. The people of Canada will remember this government for years and years, the black days of this government and the butcher from Baie Comeau.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the issue of male violence against women is the foremost and most urgent issue confronting women in our society.
In Metro Toronto from 1984 to 1989, there has been a 48.4 per cent increase in violent crime and a 62.4 per cent increase in family violence. Weapons are now used in 45.7 per cent of domestic cases, compared to 30.9 per cent in 1985. To November 30 of this year, there have been 513 family violence incidents involving firearms, compared to 465 for the whole year of 1989.
Are large urban centres unique? No. StatsCan reports that in communities with a population of 5,000 or less, the homicide rate for the last 10 years was 3.1 per 100,000, as compared to 3.14 in communities of 500,000 or more.
Security of person is a fundamental human right denied to most women in our society everywhere.

Mr. Speaker, as we are all aware, the CBC is going to announce later this hour the most severe budget cuts in its histoiy.

One employee out of ten will be out of a job, which means a total of 1,200 jobs lost. That is what this government has done, by forcing the CBC to cut its budget by more than $100 million.

The procedure provides, interestingly enough, in each supply period for the opposition to have allotted days, or opposition days, when they can raise and debate in the House the expenditures in these estimates. I wrote a letter, along with three other colleagues in the Liberal caucus, the hon. member for Burin-St. George's being one of them, and two other members, asking the clerk of that committee to cause this committee to meet. We wanted to study, among other things, issues involving Canada Post as well as the estimates.
I received a letter from the clerk of the committee, which I am willing to lay on the table of the House, which says that our committee cannot meet. The clerk is unable to make it meet as we do not have a chairman and the government will not appoint one. So in that particular case, we cannot study the estimates. There is nothing we can do about it because the government will not and has not appointed the chairman.
I am willing to table this letter in the House of Commons to prove the point. In at least that particular situation, the case is even stronger why the estimates cannot be deemed to have been reported because the committee could not have sat no matter what it had decided to do. That has been caused by an action, or rather an inaction, of the government across the way.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few comments to this debate with regard to the lack of committee meetings that has pervaded this place.
When I was first given the critic's responsibility for communications, arts and culture, which was just before the session began, I was quite anxious to have an opportunity to take part in the committee meetings that would be taking place.
Since that time, there has not been a single committee meeting, to discuss estimates, to discuss concentration of the media, to discuss the budgetary cutbacks to the CBC, to discuss nothing. I looked at the options that I had as a member in order to force the committee to meet and I ran up against exactly the same roadblock as the hon. member just pointed out.
The fact is that the communications, arts and culture committee has no chairperson. The former chairperson does not want to play chairperson any longer. We have no chairman. Therefore there is no procedural way that we can put in a legitimate request for this committee to meet to address the very important needs that we need to address.
This is an abdication of the democratic responsibility of the House and it is a shameful misuse of the privileges of the House by the government. It has to stop, and it has to stop now.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, earlier today I served notice by way of written letter that I intended to rise under the provisions of Standing Order 52 to seek the adjournment of the House for the purposes of debating the imminent closure of the CBC broadcasting facilities in a number of Canadian municipalities.
Although the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reports to Parliament through the Ministry of Communications, in fact, Mr. Speaker, as you know, it operates at arm's length from the government.
The only appropriate way for parliamentarians to direct the CBC in its use of public funds is, of course, through parliamentary debate, not through direct government intervention. While some parliamentarians, I submit, had an opportunity to debate this issue directly
with the president of the CBC this morning, they did so in a private meeting with the government caucus earlier today, that same privilege and courtesy was not extended to the members of the opposition. The president did not seek the opportunity in the morning to speak to the concerns of parliamentarians on the opposition side of the House. Nor has the right of Canadians to open public debate on this issue of national importance been fulfilled.
In summarizing, and for that reason, Sir, I ask that the House provide an opportunity for this most urgent debate to occur. For that reason, I beseech you, Sir, with the request that this house do adjourn for that purpose.

The House resumed from Monday, November 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Loiselle that Bill C-91, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act and other acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
December 5, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about this bill that seeks to amend the Financial Administration Act.
The bill, because of its fairly wide sweeping nature, gives us the opportunity to make a few points about this government's performance and, Lord knows, there is much that can be said about the performance of this government, and not very much of it complimentary.
My friend from Calgary Southeast nods his approval to every word I say. Or, is he just so glad that he is still on the backbench at this particular time and not on the frontbench where he would have to bear direct responsibility for it? He is not completely absolved of course because he is still at least nominally a supporter of the government, and I stress "nominally" because I know his commitment to his constituents and to Canada, a commitment which I suggest prevents him from being a very enthusiastic supporter of some of the things this government is doing at this particular time.
As I said, Bill C-91 seeks to amend the Financial Administration Act in several ways. It allows me the opportunity to pick up where I left off a few days ago when we were discussing another related matter. I was explaining to you, Mr. Speaker, rather concisely, as is my usual form, and to my good friend from Gander-Grand Falls and others who were in the Chamber, as he is always in the Chamber, why it was that I chose to characterize our beloved Prime Minister as a wrecking ball. I was saying that in a somewhat warped sense it was some kind of a compliment. My friend from St. John's East will know exactly what I am talking about here.
A wrecking ball is not something that is flayed without direction. That is a loose cannon. A loose cannon on a deck can do a lot of damage because it has nobody orchestrating its movements but the weather, the wind, and itself. It can go in any direction at any time, depending on the whim of the wind, the slant on the deck, and the direction of it. The result is that it can do untold damage to any above deck structure. A loose cannon is not to be confused with a wrecking ball.
A wrecking ball, contrary to the image that it conjures up, is a very precise instrument. In the right hands and with the right pre-planning it can damage, yes, but damage in a predetermined way. The controllers of that wrecking ball know exactly what it is they want done. By
Government Orders
appropriate orchestration and pre-planning, they can see that that ball does only the damage intended and no other damage. That is the basic difference between a loose cannon, I submit, and a wrecking ball.
Why, then, do I not just go all hog and call the Prime Minister a loose cannon? That would be wrong. He is no loose cannon. He is not just rolling around out of control. He knows exactly what he is up to. He is a wrecking ball, yes. He is doing damage, yes, but it is prescribed and predetermined damage. It is the damage that says, as it did recently when the government decided to reduce expenditures by $350 million, to rural Canada: "We are going to take away from you $12 million in agricultural funding". It is the damage that says to fisheries: "We are going to take away $11 million". It is the damage that says to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency: "We are going to take away $640,000". So it goes. It is that kind of pre-planned wrecking ball damage.
If we talk about fisheries-and I am delighted to see my friend, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, in the House-and about finding another $11 million, the question is: How do we find another $11 million without cutting into essential programs?
I will use an analogy that will be understood by most members of this House. Certainly it will be understood in parts of this country where they still use the soup bone to get a last bit of nourishment from the bit of beef they had the day before for dinner. I say to my friend from Gander-Grand Falls that this is the kind of analogy with which he and his people would identify with. They, like my people in Burin-St. George's, often resort to the soup bone. This is not because they are all poverty stricken, although many of them are hurting, but because they are resourceful. They do not believe in throwing away anything. The analogy I am reaching for is that however good the soup bone is and the bit of meat that might be left on it and the pot of soup it might make, you cannot have a steak dinner on a soup bone.
In the same context, you cannot find in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, money that is no longer there. You cannot have the luxury of cutting from fisheries and oceans money that is so desperately needed. Indeed, at this particular time there ought to be a

December 5, 1990

fairly massive shift of funding into fisheries and oceans and other departments.
Let me address the expenditure cuts of last week amounting to $350 million in the context that the Prime Minister brought them forward. In fairness to him, he said that these cutbacks were being implemented in relation to the expenditures we were incurring in the Persian Gulf.
He will find no argument from this member. I believe he will find no argument from any member of this Chamber that we must pay our way if we incur certain expenses in the Persian Gulf or wherever. We must have a financial plan to ensure that we are not out spending like a drunken sailor but that we are spending in a way that we know we can pay the bills when they become due. I have no argument whatsoever with the marvellous concept that if we are to incur expenditures in the Persian Gulf or wherever, we ought to be there with a plan as to how we are to pay the bills.
I also say to the Prime Minister and others who are saddled with the need to find ways to pay the bills in the Persian Gulf, that these are commitments that every Canadian would proudly stand behind. There is a need to ensure that our interests in the Persian Gulf are adequately protected. However there is a but.
I understand that the government has to find ways to meet the financial obligations in the Persian Gulf, and with that I have no argument. I have great difficulty with the way it is being done. I believe it is unconscionable that at a time when fisheries is hurting it cuts even more deeply into the soup bone I mentioned earlier. At a time when agriculture is on its knees, the government is wanting to take another $12 million. At a time when the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is already strapped for funds, it is reaching out once more to take money from it. At a time when we need infrastructure and expenditures in transport in Atlantic Canada, it is reaching in and taking out $31 million. At a time when the government has already cut the guts out of its commitment to unemployment insurance, it is now going to the Department of Employment and Immigration and reaching in for another $25 million.
I have no difficulty with the idea that there is a need to meet our commitments in the gulf. I have much difficulty
with the way it is being done. If the government wants a way to find that $500 million, it is fairly simple. It can renege on that cowardly and secret commitment it made to the Americans. The former member for York-Peel, Mr. Sinclair Stevens, mentioned it a few days ago in the press. He publicly confirmed what we have been saying for four or five years, that there had to be a cooked deal on interest rates. There is no other explanation why our interest rates are 5 percentage points higher. I say to my friend from St. John's East that there is no explanation for that. I have always understood the idea that they ought to be maybe marginally higher.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: You told us that we can't manage the economy, and we stabilized the interest rate.
I missed the brunt of what my friend from St. John's East was saying. I invite him one more time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: You never understood me.
I understand him all too well. I just do not agree with him. There is the difference. I even admire the way he defends his stands, however wrongly arrived at.
That's the Christmas season.

As I was saying, the member has no worries about his intellectual stature. It is well up there. I have no difficulty with that at all. The physical height was not of his doing, but what he has done with what he had is marvellous and I congratulate him.
Let us get back to the subject at hand. I have something to say to the hon. member for St. John's East and to others. My good friend from Burlington is chafing at the bit to respond to what I have to say, but would he hear first what I have to say. There is no earthly reason he can give this House as to why our interest rates ought to be 5 percentage points higher than they are in the States.
I can buy the idea that maybe they ought to be marginally higher, a point or point and a half, to attract some investment over the border. However, they ought not to be 5 per cent. There had to be some convoluted reason why they were, and Sine Stevens gave us that convoluted reason the other day when he said publicly that there was a deal back there, something that many of us have felt for a long time. Otherwise, in the absence of

an undertaking to artificially keep those rates high, there is no market reason why they would be as high. There had to be tampering, and that is what Sine Stevens told us the other day. I understand that his former colleagues now want to disown him on that, but that is between him and them. I am not here to make the brief for him. What I am saying is that unwittingly or otherwise he let the cat out of the bag the other day. We now know. We now have confirmed what a lot of us suspected for a long time.
I come to the point as it relates to today's debate. If the government wants to find $500 million or whatever amount to finance its gulf operation, I have a suggestion for it. Cut interest rates by 1 per cent, and it will find not $500 million but $1.7 billion, because that is what will be generated. As my hon. friend from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell well knows, what will be generated by 1 percentage point cut in the interest rate will be $1.7 billion.
Let me say it differently. Our commitment in terms of deficit reduction will go down. Our required commitment will go down by $1.7 billion just by cutting our interest rates 1 per cent. If the government wants a sure way, a quick way and a painless way of paying the bills in the gulf, I give that one to my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, without charge.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Carried. Let's do it now.

My friend from Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, being a charitable man, jumps to the conclusion that the government will take it because it is sensible. I say to him that had it been of the inclination long ago to take things that are sensible, we would be in a lot less trouble in this country than we are.
The reason for which we are in the financial mess we are in is that this government paid lip service right back in the fall of 1984 when the minister brought down his first budget after the September election. It is worth reading. I went back the other night and read it again. I got a kick out of Grimm's Fairy Tales when I was younger, but this one really turns you on. If you want to read a modem day myth, you should hear what the Minister of Finance actually said with a straight face. He said to all of Canada back in late 1984 what he was going to do to bring down the deficit, how it was going to be a
Government Orders
new world, how it was going to be marvellous out there, and everything was going to be hunky-dory.
We are in 1990 and we know what hunky-dory is. Hunky-dory is an unemployment rate of 18 per cent in Newfoundland, higher than it has been in years. The unemployment rate is skyrocketing all over the country. People are being pummelled in terms of their own unemployment insurance. People are being pummelled in terms of their jobs in the fishery. The government allowed overfishing to get completely out of hand before it even began to pay lip service.
I stood in this House in December 1988, soon after the November election that year, and I raised the question of foreign overfishing. My hon. friend from St. John's West, the Minister for International Trade and the then Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the now Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, laughed me out of the place. They literally laughed me out of the Chamber because I would suggest that there was a problem. More to the point, they tried to laugh me out of the place because I suggested that the solution was to start getting tough with the European Community about the overfishing by Spain and Portugal in particular.
That year, 1988, was the fourth year of scandalous, criminal overfishing. The Portuguese and the Spanish as part of the European Community were allowed in 1985 to take 23,200 tonnes. In that year, they took 172,000 tonnes. The next year they took 12 times their quota, and so it went on. Four years after, I was the first person in four years to raise it in this House. Not one person raised it publicly in 1985, 1986, 1987 or 1988; it was not raised publicly. I raised it here for the first time in December 1988, and I was told I did not know what I was talking about.
Mr. Speaker, I now ask you to go back and read the words of the member for St. John's West and the minister of fisheries as he then was. Then read the press release put out last week by the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans from New Brunswick and the Minister for International Trade. Do you know what they said? Almost word for word, they said what I was saying in December 1988 about the nature of the problem over there and what needs to be done about it. They were saying what my hon. friend from Gander-Grand Falls has been saying and what my hon. friend from Bona-vis-ta-Trinity-Conception has been saying. We three, not to ignore the others from Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada, sit literally on the ocean; our ridings sit facing the ocean. What happens out there very seriously im-

Government Orders
pacts the ability of our people to earn a livelihood because their livelihood is the ocean. If the Portuguese, the Spanish and the French take it, our people cannot have the same fish the next day. You cannot catch it twice.
If a government of whatever political stripe stands idly by, or aids and abets the process by silence for four years, then our people suffer and our plants close, not because the resource is not there but because somebody else is getting their claws on it before our people do, aided and abetted by a government that ought to be protecting our interests.
Mr. Speaker, I see from your signal that I am getting close to the end of my allotted time. I know that before you became a very able Acting Speaker, you were a very able football player and I suspect that some of the signals I am getting now are about football. I do not know much about football, but I think the general message is I should sit down fairly soon. I will try to do that within a minute. My friend from St. John's is much more direct. He wants more.
I am sure he will recognize the truth of what I said about the overfishing and the fact that, as they say in French, Mieux vaut tard que jamais, better late than never. Even if my friend from St. John's West and the Minister of Fisheries have come lately to the job, lately to the need, lately to the realization that something has to be done about the overfishing, I say to them, better late than never. A lot of damage has been done, a lot of jobs have been lost, but at least by getting in now, five years late, they are not going to be 10 years late, and for that we can be thankful.
This Financial Administration Act needs amendment. All the amendments in the world are absolutely useless, absolutely beside the point, if we do not have in government somebody who administers that act competently. That right now is the crux of the problem. It is why our people are suffering. It is why the government is going in all the wrong directions to fund our overseas commitment in the Persian Gulf.
If it would instead get a sensible interest rate policy, fire John Crow and get someone there who understands how people are hurting, who understands that government is not first a business. It is an enterprise which
ought to look after the needs of people. If government were a business alone, we would not need a government. We would just have one of the big multinational corporations run the whole thing for us. We need government, but by that, we need a government worthy of the name. That is our problem right now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burin-St. George's in the course of his comments made the remark that someone had said to him that he did not know what he was talking about. I have to concur with whoever that was.
In the course of his remarks he said that Mr. Stevens had made some comment about interest rates. He should read the newspapers again. There was no comment made about interest rates at all. Mr. Stevens apparently was reflecting on a conversation he had with the former Secretary of Commerce of the United States, Mr. Baldrige. They were talking about the level of the dollar, not the level of interest rates.
They were not talking about interest rates at all and that was confirmed by the Minister for International Trade of the day who is now in the Senate, the Minister of Finance, the chief negotiator for the government, the deputy negotiator for the government and several others who were involved in it. There was no mention of interest rates whatever, no mention of the dollar whatever.

I thank my friend from Burlington. As usual he is half right. Let me deal with the first half first and then I will come to the matter about the interest rate versus the dollar. On the first half he said that I had said that I was told that I did not know what I was talking about. The answer to his question as to who told me was in my earlier speech. The member for St. John's West and the then Minister of Fisheries said I did not know what I was talking about when I talked about the damage overfishing was doing.
If he wants to stand in front of 100,000 fishermen in Atlantic Canada and tell them there is no overfishing, then he had better try harder and shout louder because the message is going to be difficult getting through when people sit in their homes in Seal Cove-I know he does not want to hear this, but I am going to tell him anyway-people sit in their homes in Seal Cove. They
December 5, 1990

see their stocks being raped by fishermen from France, Spain and Portugal. Yes, I knew what I was talking about. Whether the member for Burlington agrees that I knew does not bother me. Let me thank him and say that he is absolutely right on the second. I made an error. I was inadvertently saying interest rates. Of course, what Mr. Stevens had to say was about the dollar. I thank him very much for correcting the record on that.
I believe he will agree that if you follow the argument through that I was making, it applies equally to the dollar as it does to interest rates because the two matters are related.
The argument basically was that there had been a convoluted undertaking by the Government of Canada to a foreign power to give that government a say, leverage, in our internal affairs. The level of our dollar is wiping out the exports in Newfoundland on fish, pulp and paper, and mining. It is wiping them out because of the level of the dollar.
Now we know what we have suspected for a long time, that our jobs in Newfoundland and elsewhere in Atlantic Canada-wherever there are resource industries with exports flowing from them-are being sacrificed because according to Mr. Stevens, and confirmed by the minister as the member for Burnaby has reminded us, there was a deal to artificially peg the level of the dollar up around 85 cents to 90 cents-85 at the moment but the objective was close to 90.

Mr. Speaker, near the end of the member's speech, he mentioned the word "competence", I believe it was. I am honestly surprised that anyone who was in a Liberal government with any knowledge of the spending habits of that party could even talk about restraint.
Let me just give you a couple of figures, Mr. Speaker. In the five years prior to us assuming power in 1984, the average level of spending by the Liberal government, excluding interest rates, if I recall correctly, was over 14 per cent. It doubles in about five years at that rate of expenses. The previous five years to that was a little over 10 per cent as I recall. The previous five years to that, again under the Liberal government was over 17 per cent a year.
In six years, our average annual increase has been a marvellous 3.5 per cent, under the rate of inflation. We never hear them mention that type of thing because they are too embarrassed about their 15-year record-and they should be-when spending got totally out of control by that previous government.
We have turned from an operating deficit to an operating surplus, a turnaround of about $25 billion. They have the nerve to question the competence of the track record of this government. I wish he would look back on his own and maybe we could chat a bit about that when I see him in the gym tomorrow morning.

I say to my friend for Markham- Whitchurch-Stouffville all of that was fair play except the last sentence. The last sentence is getting dangerously into my personal life when he talks about our being in the gym at seven o'clock in the morning trying to keep in shape. He is very good company. We do not always agree, as I am sure you have just seen, but he is very good company.
I thank the hon. member also for bringing to the debate-and this is the beauty of this period, this 10-minute question and answer-it puts another flavour on the debate. He has brought the debate to another side of the issue.
He talks about not having the courage-whatever word he used-to put forward the argument. No. He knows the process very well. My job is not to stand here and praise the government for any good things it might do. It is not what I am sent here for at all. I am sent here to keep the government accountable. I fully expect that if the government does some good things I can depend

December 5, 1990
Government Orders
on the competence of the gentleman from Markham to make sure that it is known. Listen to our title-Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. We are here to poke holes in what that crowd does, and it is an easy job because there are so many places to poke the holes. We are not here as acolytes for the fellow from Baie Comeau.
Do not ever be under the impression that I am going to be out singing the praises of this government. If it does something that is particularly laudable, I will get up and swallow my pride and congratulate them. But I do not find it laudable that it went off and cooked the Canadian dollar up around 85 cents to satisfy the Americans on the free trade issue. I do not find it laudable that high interest rates are artificially pegged. My people in Burin-St. George's and elsewhere are hurting because they are paying a much higher mortgage than they ought to be.
The gentleman from Markham and I are not really at odds to the degree that he might suggest. He happens to be in a party where he has to be an acolyte. He has to say all the good things about that crowd and shut up about the rest. That is his problem, not mine.
In my case, I happen to be part of the Official Opposition whose job it is to point out that the cutbacks this government has inflicted over the past six years are hurting the poor, are robbing people of their jobs. If he thinks I am going to stand here and ignore what it is doing to my people, I will not. He might shout, but he might keep his cool as well because the effect will be the same on me.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very short question. First of all, I want to congratulate my colleague for his excellent remarks. I am sure I speak on behalf of most members of this House who probably inadvertently forgot to mention that when they rose to ask a question of my colleague.
Does he not find that the argument of the government that it needed the supplementary estimates in order to pay for the gulf war just a little shallow when, in fact, far more money will be spent to administer the GST than will ever be used in any effort that is presently contemplated in the Persian Gulf? Does he not agree with me
that the funds that will be used to collect the GST, just that surplus portion of $365 million, could be far better used to assist either the fishermen in his riding or the unemployed people in Hawkesbury and elsewhere in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell because he hits the nail right on the head, as he usually does. Of course, it is a very shallow argument. When he mentions the GST, he reminds me, because he has made the first argument so well, I need not repeat it. Let me give him a parallel argument which reinforces the very point that he makes rhetorically in his question.
I heard the other day that the government wants to pay all the people out there the tax credit before Christmas. But it cannot do it unless the big, bad Liberal senators stop filibustering and pass the bill. The government cannot pay or draw money until the bill is passed.
Now, what kind of double-talk is that when the same government that cannot pay tax credits to people who are wondering whether they will have a Christmas or not, sitting on the edge of their chairs waiting to know if they will get the tax return in time for Christmas, and are being held to ransom, being blackmailed by this government, the same government that cannot find the money to pay the tax credit, is actually spending equivalent amounts of money renting four floors in the hotel over here to administer the GST? It had to pay money down for that, did it not? It is spending millions on TV. What Canadian, even those waiting for the cheques out there, has not seen those foolish ads on TV? Do you think they get them for nothing? They cost money. How come? I ask you, Mr. Speaker-and I am just about through-how come the government that cannot find money to pay the tax credit before the bill goes through can find globs of money to rent four floors of a hotel to administer the GST, and for all the other foolish reasons, the hot line and so on. What hypocrisy! What shallowness!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The hon. member for Essex-Windsor. I have to recognize the NDP. The last five speakers have been from the Liberal Party so I will recognize the hon. member for Essex-Windsor.
December 5, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I am spurred, I guess, by the comments of the previous speaker and by the question which the hon. member for Burlington put before this House with respect to the whole question of the value of our dollar and the relationship of that to the free trade agreement.
This is, of course, something which is, one would have to concede, only tendentiously connected to the piece of legislation which is in front of us. But since it has come up in debate, I wanted to add just a few comments in respect of some of the exchanges which have been taking place.
We have not had a chance in the House actually to debate the rather extraordinary comments which a former Minister of Industry in this government made this past weekend with respect to a gentleman's agreement, as he put it, to see to it that the value of the Canadian dollar was raised quite significantly. There was some exchange which took place in Question Period and I happened to be in my constituency at that time. It has been only since my return that I have had a chance to see some of the comments of the Minister of Finance with respect to these comments of the former Minister of Industry of the Conservative government, Mr. Stevens.
Mr. Stevens suggested, on the basis of his discussions with Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige, who was essentially in many respects Mr. Stevens' counterpart in the U.S. administration. He suggested in 1985, according to Mr. Stevens, that it was going to be essential that the dollar be raised in value if a free trade deal was going to take place.
This suggestion by the former Minister of Industry in the Conservative government was met by the Minister of Finance with statements of complete dismissal. On Monday, he put it in the following terms. He said:
- that the statement was absurd speculation, but it is simply also not true.
He went on from that to say:
I would remind my hon. friend that Mr. Stevens was basing his speculative comments on a conversation that he had with a man who was not involved in the negotiations and a conversation that was held some two years before the final negotiations were completed.
Government Orders
That might seem to put an end to this whole issue very clearly and to any speculation that might exist on this side of the House. In tracing this issue through the past five years-since the time that the supposed conversation took place between Mr. Stevens and the U.S. Commerce Secretary-we found that in fact this was not the only occasion on which this question of the value of the Canadian dollar was raised in prominent terms in the context of discussion of the Canadian trade deal, not by Canadians, not by the opposition attempting to suggest that something underhanded was taking place, but instead by senior Americans who were in fact, unlike the reference in Mr. Wilson's statement, deeply involved in the negotiations with respect to free trade. These questions were raised, not just by such people, but they were raised after' negotiations had already started with the United States with respect to a free trade deal.
Unfortunately, many of us would have to put a lack of strong faith into the recollections, five years after the fact, of a former minister of industry of this government who, after all, did have to resign in rather unfortunate circumstances. Despite our scepticism about that minister, the fact of the matter is that in the aftermath of that 1985 period there continued to be right up to 1987, the year in which the free trade negotiations were concluded, continuing comments on the part of key American officials with respect to this issue.
I want to note some of these for Canadians who are perhaps perplexed at the very quick way in which the serious suggestions of the former minister of industry were dismissed by the Minister of Finance. I will first quote from the person who was the negotiator from the United States, Peter Murphy, who wrote a memo in April of 1986. This was considerably after the discussions with Mr. Baldrige. He directed this memo to the members of the Canadian task force senior staff, that is, the people who were in charge of negotiating with the Canadian delegation with respect to free trade.
The memo came from Ambassador Murphy and the subject was Canadian negotiations. It stated: "Now that we have squeaked by in the Senate, the hard part starts. We have to prepare for the negotiations." He went on to review a number of key points which would be important to consider in the course of the negotiations. He noted only six points, so this was one of quite a small number of important points that he made. One of the important

Government Orders
issues to consider was "the direction and situation of exchange rates over the last 10 years, and efforts, if any, to change it, both in Canada and the United States." That might be seen simply as a small point and simply a review of what past exchange rates had been.
It is interesting that at the same time, virtually, in fact about a month later, James Baker, the United States Treasury Secretary at that point, had this to say. We all know that he is now the Foreign Secretary, but at that point he was the Treasury Secretary. The following appeared in a story by Alan Toulin, who now works for The Financial Post: "Yesterday Baker told a Senate committee that entry of Canada and Italy into the G-5 could swing the spotlight on to the economic policies of both countries and require them to meet policy goals set by the G-5."
Again, it was a relatively innocuous comment, one might think, until further on in the story one gets the following comment: "'Re-evaluating the Canadian dollar could also figure in the free trade negotiations slated to begin today,' U.S. Senator Daniel Evans said yesterday in a CBC interview."
One might think that this, again, is a relatively insignificant act, but what is fascinating is that these kinds of comments continue throughout 1986. In a story from September 10, 1986 written by Jonathan Ferguson who reported on U.S. Secretary Malcolm Baldrige speaking before a committee of the House of Representatives in Washington. This is precisely the same person who the former minister of industry in this Conservative government said in 1985 had told him that it was essential to get the Canadian dollar higher. A year later, September 10, 1986, after the free trade negotiations had started, he is saying precisely the same thing and I quote from this story by Jonathan Ferguson: "U.S. Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige told a committee of the House of Representatives in Washington yesterday that an increase in the value of the Canadian dollar would help ease the record U.S. trade deficit."
Well, again, one might say this is just an idle comment by somebody who was not deeply involved in these issues.
Then there is a front page story from The Ottawa Citizen of November 21, 1986 in which Peter Murphy, who was the chief United States negotiator in these free trade negotiations, speaks out. This story, written by Wendy Warburton, starts as follows: '"The U.S. Congress would likely want changes in Canada's exchange rate, the value of the Canadian dollar compared to the U.S. dollar, before it would pass a free trade agreement,' American trade negotiator Peter Murphy said Thursday."
He went on to say that this was being looked at by Treasury Secretary James Baker. That is a direct quote. "Secretary Baker is dealing with that, but what you cannot do is separate that in the mind-set of the Congress who will vote for a deal, that is for a free trade deal, or vote against it". Here we have Mr. Murphy talking in these terms.
We followed up on some of these comments by these various people who have been noted here. There are, for instance, Malcolm Baldrige's comments from the testimony which he presented to the House of Representatives which has been quoted here from September. It is quite clear. He is talking about the United States dollar and he said: "The U.S. dollar remains strong against the currencies of countries accounting for over half of our total trade, including our largest trading partner, Canada". He went on to say: "We are seeking discussions with a number of countries on the exchange rate issue. Progress there would be beneficial".
James Baker, in his testimony to the committee on finance in the United States Senate said: "There is not a lot we can do about those countries that tie their currencies to ours", and he goes on to talk about other countries, "but I think the fact there has been a depreciation of the dollar, that is the U.S. dollar, will help our trading relationship with those countries by putting more pressure on their markets and less on ours".
Finally, I would stress that despite the fact that Mr. Reisman, the Canadian negotiator in 1987, said: "We will not discuss the dollar in any way, shape or form", January 17, 1987, he did this in the aftermath of the comments by Mr. Murphy, the U.S. negotiator, in which he made it quite clear that the value of the Canadian dollar was quite important in consideration of the U.S. trade deal.
December 5, 1990

I have to conclude with two observations. The first observation is that Mr. Reisman walked out of the negotiations at a very late stage. It was never entirely clear and he never entirely indicated why he had walked out of those negotiations. I wonder if it was because something which he had said would not be on the table suddenly became crucial in the latter stages of that negotiation. I wonder if that is the case.
Finally, I think we have to conclude that Mr. Wilson's comments that this is not something to consider seriously, what Mr. Sinclair Stevens suggested last Sunday, because it took place well before the trade negotiations started and because it was based on conversations with someone who was not even in those negotiations, that that denial in fact itself holds no water. We can see from these comments that I have quoted to the House today that after that time, in fact after the negotiations had started with the United States, senior figures on the United States side, who were in charge of those negotiations, such as Peter Murphy and James Baker, did in fact talk directly and in terms of joining the question of the value of our dollar with whether or not the free trade deal would be accepted. Given the fact that they spoke in those terms, is there in fact any reason to reject the suggestions which Mr. Stevens made this past Sunday?
I think there may not be a clear smoking gun here, but there certainly is a great deal of evidence from the period when negotiations were taking place, from people who were part of those negotiations that in fact the United States saw the value of our dollar as a key component with respect to the free trade deal.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret the hon. member's time has expired. Questions or comments.

Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the contribution that the member from Windsor has made to this debate.
There is no question in my mind that the exchange rates between Canada and the United States were a key component throughout the trade discussions between Canada and the United States. I wonder how a so-called free trade agreement can possibly exist, unless there are arrangements made to stabilize the relationships between currencies.
Government Orders
As I recall from the discussions we had in British Columbia around the softwood lumber problem and the threat of American trade retaliation against our softwood lumber, the currency was the major issue.
Even though the Americans used the excuse of the stumpage rates in a number of Canadian provinces, American senators and congressmen whom I met when the Gibbons committee travelled to Vancouver indicated to us that, when they saw Canadian lumber coming into places like Little Rock, Arkansas and selling at a price, because of the value of the Canadian dollar, far below what Arkansas lumber fetched in the Little Rock market, their sawmills shut down.
Their lumber workers were out of work, and they, as U.S. congressmen and senators, were going to take any action necessary, legal or otherwise, in order to reverse the situation.
The specific problem that they identified was the decline in Canadian currency relative to the American currency. That precipitated a retaliation by the American softwood lumber industry against Canada.
I cannot see how it is possible that free trade discussions took place between Canada and the U.S. without some currency pegging arrangements being made, whether it was an insistence by the Americans that the government in Canada raised interest rates in order to keep the value of our dollar propped, or whether some other arrangements were made behind the curtain between the Conservative government's negotiators and the American negotiators.
I just cannot understand a free trade arrangement existing without some currency pegging arrangements existing at the same time. I would appreciate if the member would respond to that.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the member is quite right in pointing to the fact that the exchange rate was the common issue which American politicians, in discussing trade issues with Canada throughout that whole period, emphasized in their discussions.
We certainly found that to be the case. For example, when a delegation of American congressmen came here to talk about grain issues, it was the low value of the Canadian dollar at that stage which was of particular concern to them.

December 5, 1990
Government Orders
Precisely the same thing is true with respect to the objections under the auto pact which were put forward from Michigan. The various congressmen and senators from the state of Michigan who were concerned about Canadian exports under the auto pact into the United States emphasized the low value of the Canadian dollar.
I think that one has that set of evidence to look at. One has the set of evidence that I have talked about today. One has as well the fact that ever since the trade deal has come into effect, a gap has grown between interest rates in this country and in the United States, which is something which we have never seen historically in this country at that kind of level.
We are talking about a percentage point difference of from four to five percentage points which, given the fact that inflation rates are very similar between the two countries, means that the only conceivable consequence of that huge gap in interest rates would be to raise the value of the Canadian dollar.
We have not seen a reduction in the Canadian inflation rate relative to the American inflation rate. What we have seen is what all these people were suggesting was necessary for the free trade deal and that is a marked increase in the value of the Canadian dollar from the level of about 73 cents, which it was in 1985, to the level of approximately 86 cents, which it presently is.
Of course, that is damaging in the extreme to all of our exporters no matter which part of the country they are in; British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, or Atlantic Canada. It is an incredibly damaging blow to our potential as a country to provide jobs and incomes.
The facts, therefore, speak for themselves. It is those facts that we have to look at in judging whether or not Mr. Stevens' comments this past weekend should be taken seriously or not. Do the facts conform with what Mr. Stevens suggested? Unfortunately, for the government, and unfortunately for its suggestions that this is not the case, the facts indeed do conform exactly with what one would expect to have taken place if Mr. Stevens had indeed been telling the truth.
I have to say that the statement of this past week demonstrates yet again the irresponsibility of this government which has led to the damage which this economy is now suffering, the first made in Canada recession which Canada has ever experienced.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I understand that I am the last speaker on this particular bill before the House which is- the Financial Administration Act.
I have just a couple of points concerning provisions in the bill that are, quite frankly, bad legislation for the people of Canada. One of them deals with collection agencies. One deals with saltfish, and the other one could deal with air traffic control centres in Vancouver and in eastern Canada.
The first one concerns collection agencies. Clause 5 of the bill enables the Government of Canada to hire collection agencies in any department, in any Crown corporation, in any agency of the federal government to collect moneys that are owed the Government of Canada. Collection agencies.
The Minister of Justice is sitting here. The minister knows the procedure today whereby a department of government collects it money.
First, a person is given a reasonable opportunity to make the payment. If that fails and if the person defaults on his or her payments, then perhaps through a third party attachment the wages are attached. Or, the person who is due money by that agency or that department has it taken off a bit at a time.
That is the standard procedure used by the Government of Canada and its departments. In legislation passed by this Chamber we have clauses in certain bills that terminate moneys owed to the Government of Canada over certain periods of time. In other words, there are two ways in which something can be forgiven. One is, in certain legislation, if it imposes undue hardship on the person involved. Second, in some legislation there is a time limit. In other words, in some legislation it is set out that moneys cannot be collected beyond three years from the date at which the individual was notified that he or she owed money to the department.
Now that is the jurisprudence we have in Canada today. That is reasonable law. What is the Minister of Justice and the Government of Canada doing by putting forward this proposed legislation and saying throughout the legislation that collection agencies are now to be used by the Government of Canada, not only in the restricted sense that we have today to collect the student loans that are overdue but in every agency of the

Government of Canada and in every department? Now, circumventing the system, we have the imposition of collection agencies. Shame on the Minister of Justice for permitting this to pass through cabinet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I don't chew my cabbage twice.

I hope that is on the record. The Minister of Justice has just made a statement; she says she does not chew her cabbage twice. I hope that she chews it at least once. This entire bill is enough to give anybody indigestion.
The second portion of the bill which is really objectionable is a new imposition on Crown corporations listed in schedule 3 of part X of the Financial Administration Act. There are three schedules, Mr. Speaker, as you know.
The first schedule includes government departments. The second schedule includes Crown corporations that are part of government departments, and the third schedule is wholly owned Crown corporations, owned by the Government of Canada. This bill imposes upon those Crown corporations an obligation to collect money and have a reasonable expectation that the corporation will pay dividends.
In other words, the whole intent of the legislation is that the Crown corporation becomes, through another part of the bill and using user fees in some cases, a money maker. That is the philosophy of the Government of Canada. CBC is not included in schedule 3 of the Financial Administration Act because it is considered to be a cultural institution which remains autonomous from section 3.
What will happen if we take the established Crown corporations of today to deal with the natural resources of Canada? I use as an example the Canadian Saltfish Corporation. Last week half of the people employed by that Crown corporation received their lay-off notices. The function of that Crown corporation was to provide marketing, to be the sole buyer and marketer of what we call saltfish, which is a fish that is cut open and then there is salt put on it. It is dried with salt on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is that a recipe?

Back in my day, we used to dry them on what we called flakes, but now it is automatic drying machines.
The Canadian Saltfish Corporation fulfilled that vital function. Now it is in trouble because it owes a lot of money to the Government of Canada. That is a relatively new phenomenon. What caused it? The Government of Canada caused it. The Government of Canada, to my way of thinking, in my estimation, caused the crisis in the fishing industry in Canada.
How did it do that?

The member asks how the government caused the problem. Today I received an update on the numbers of licences issued to foreign interests in Canadian waters so far this year. It comes to 135 factory ship licences issued to Cuba, Japan, U.S.S.R., Bulgaria, Norway, Poland, and the U.S.A. That is an increase over last year. That is an increase over the year before last.
Who caused the crisis in the fishery in eastern Canada? If we have a larger fleet from a foreign nation fishing inside our 200-mile zone, licensed by the Government of Canada, a larger offshore fleet than we have in Canada, then we know that something is wrong. I am not talking about outside the 200-mile zone that the hon. member spoke about a few moments ago. I was going to mention to him about the Namibia connection, a recent phenomenon in Canada. Namibia, a country in the southern portion of Africa, declared about three weeks ago that it was going to tell every foreign nation to get out of its waters. It did it. Imagine, the Government of Namibia. I checked and I found that there were about 100 factory ships from Europe in its zone in Namibia. Namibia threatened them. They left about two and one-half weeks ago, and they steamed right up through the Atlantic Ocean. Where did they go, some of them? They went right up, off the east coast of Canada, and they started to fish just outside the 200-mile zone in the shallow water.
Our search planes and survey planes for the last two weeks have been flying over these ships. They take photographs. They have very sophisticated machinery aboard to observe what these vessels are doing. They discovered that some of the ships that were chased from Namibia were out off the east coast of Canada, and they were catching a type of flatfish. They will destroy that particular species. I am not talking about the disaster that is happening outside, because even countries in

Government Orders
Africa that do not have our expertise in the fishery and do not have advanced fishing technology in place, are kicking out those foreign nations. Those foreign boats do not have very many places to go now, so one of the places they pick on is our Canadian east coast.
I am not talking about outside 200 miles, because we do not have jurisdiction, but we have jurisdiction for these licences granted to Cuba, Japan, the U.S.S.R., Bulgaria, Norway, Poland, and the U.S.A. We have jurisdiction tomorrow when a Japanese vessel comes in to port in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and gets from fisheries and oceans tomorrow afternoon a licence to fish what we commonly call turbot inside our 200-mile zone in areas called 2-G and 2-H off the Labrador coast.
What does that have to do with the bill? That has everything to do with the bill, because the Canadian Saltfish Corporation is paying for the follies of the Government of Canada. It is in a position where it owes money. It is being disbanded. Why else would the Government of Canada issue half or 50 per cent lay-off notices to all its staff in eastern Canada? It is an outrage.
Another portion of the bill authorizes the collection of user fees from the federal government. Imagine one government department charging another government department for use of its services. That is what it says in this bill. Another portion of the bill gives authority to charge provincial governments user fees for their services.
In the last intervention I said that I would mention in conclusion the authority given, as the government had announced prior to this bill, to government departments to collect revenues and to use those revenues as expenditures in their own departments. That is what it does in section 12 of the act. It allows a department to do it. It says that a department may be authorized to do it.
We are faced today in Canada with the probable closure of air traffic control services in western Canada, in British Columbia, and in the far east of our great country. We are facing that because the Government of Canada and the Auditor General, I believe, determined
that the work being done in those control centres could be done in a control centre in downtown Montreal.
That is one side of the picture, but that department of the Government of Canada collects revenues that far exceed their expenditures. What happens to those revenues? They go into what we call the Consolidated Revenue Fund. They do not go into the Department of Transport to keep these operations going. If we examine the figures of air traffic control stations in British Columbia and in eastern Canada, in Newfoundland or New Brunswick, we would discover an interesting fact. The system is that a foreign aircraft carrier which comes within a national airspace pays a fee for the air traffic control services it gets. It is about $85 per initial contact. That is the way it is worded. Then it pays another fee, about $501 believe-it used to be $40-for what we used to call radio services. That is when you speak to somebody about weather conditions and the like.
The average fee is $100 per initial contact for these trans-Pacific and trans-oceanic flights. There are about 500 a day on average, west coast, and east coast. That would cost approximately $50,000 a day. Air traffic control generates about $15 million to $20 million a year in eastern and western Canada. That money goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund. They make more than they spend. They are not only making their salaries, they are making double their salaries. But that does not show up in the department. That is not what this means. What this means is that where the government so wishes, a government department may be encouraged to charge fees which will then become a part of a pot of money within that department that can be spent as they see fit.
The legislation, Mr. Speaker, is incomplete. The legislation should say that each government department which generates revenue will receive that revenue and will be responsible for that revenue.
In conclusion, let me say that this is a very bad piece of legislation. It is a terrible piece of legislation. It will increase charges on the general public, on provincial governments, and it will lead the Government of Canada down some very poor paths as far as collecting money is concerned from a lot of poor people in this country.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak to this motion that I have put forward.
What my amendment will do is restore the 48-hour time period for the removal of fishing gear, especially lobster traps, from the water. When I was reading the bill, this clause eliminating the 48-hour grace period was one that stuck in my mind.
When I went home to Prince Edward Island and spoke to the lobster fishermen in my riding, I asked them how this would affect them and received the same reply over and over. "It just won't work", they said. What happens when the weather is bad? What happens if the fisheries

December 5, 1990
Government Orders
officer will not let their gear stay in the water past the closing time of the season?
I told the fishermen that I was not sure what would happen but I would bring their concerns to the committee hearings and to the House of Commons. On two separate occasions I raised the issue in committee and both times my questions and the questions of my fishermen were not answered.
When we heard the assistant deputy minister, Mr. Hache, before the committee, I asked him if it would follow that at the end of the lobster season the traps, buoys and all would have to be out of the water; if the season ends on Saturday, everything must be removed by Saturday, which the ADM responded, that is correct. Later on, I asked Mr. Hache again, if we have a stormy day on Saturday, unless the fisheries officer desires, the traps would have to come out on Friday. I can see where this would create a problem in the lobster fishery where we come from. We have always had a couple of days, 48 hours, to remove the traps from the water. Again, the ADM responded by saying, "This is correct, Mr. Chairman. There has always been an additional day or two, depending on the weather, for the fishermen to haul their gear at the end of the season".
The government has gone on and on about how this amendment to the bill will allow more flexibility in the removal of gear. Indeed, I must have heard the word hundreds of times from the government in committee. However, fishermen in my riding see this as being anything but flexible. Fishermen say that it leaves them at the mercy of the fisheries officer who may or may not look kindly upon the fishermen. Fishermen are afraid of being put in the position that they can be harassed.
During the committee hearings we heard from witnesses who said that fisheries officers are also being harassed and I agree. There are fisheries officers who are being harassed by fishermen who deliberately break the law. However, there are instances where fishermen are also harassed by fisheries officers.
This clause which says that "a fisheries officer may permit" is just another way for our fishermen to be harassed. The problem is they may or may not permit them to leave their traps in the water for another 48 hours or if it is going to be stormy on the day the season
closes, they could be forced to remove their traps possibly a day early.
It is my belief that the government's amendment to this section of the act is unnecessary. I asked the government officials if there were any problems under the old section, and they did not give me one example. They could not give me an example of any time this 48-hour grace period that our lobster fishermen had in order to have a reasonable amount of time at the end of the season to remove their traps caused difficulties.
Why was this done by the government? There is no answer. I think it could cause a problem for our fishermen. The fisheries officer might decide to give them the time, and he might not. Indeed, most fisheries officers that I deal with, or know, certainly would.
It puts the responsibility on the fishery officer, and the word "may" in the clause is very important: "They may, or they may not."
The official from the department could not point out a case. An old quote says: "If it ain't broke, don't fix it." I think this is the situation in this case. There is not a problem, so why do we here in this House create a problem for the lobster fishermen?
This government amendment is unnecessary and unwarranted. The fishermen in my riding say this will limit their flexibility in removing their gear. Of course, it certainly will complicate their flexibility.
My amendment will prevent harassment and provide greater flexibility by restoring the 48-hour time limit for the removal of fishing gear.
I urge the government members, some of whom truly understand how hard the fishermen work and how difficult it is on the sea to not place this extra burden on the fishermen and let's leave the 48-hour time period that we have had over the last number of years and treat our fishermen with respect.

and pollution prevention". It will also provide for a statistical summary of conviction under section 40 of the act.
It is very important that be included, because all of the witnesses who appeared before our committee agree- and it certainly has been a subject of public debate in British Columbia-about the need to ensure that the Fisheries Act and its rules and regulations are followed and complied with in the Pacific region and, of course, in the inland waters and on the east coast because there is concern that that in fact has not happened.
I asked questions of the witnesses based on the information and background material provided by the minister. In 1988, of some 959 fines in the Pacific region, 11 related to habitat protection and there was not a witness who thought that that adequately reflected the concerns that we have about protecting our salmon habitat on the west coast. By calling upon the minister to ensure that we have an annual report on this section, it is going to make it very clear for all members of the House and the general public to see exactly how we are dealing with that situation.
I am pleased with the government support. Tuesday, in the Environment Committee, the Minister of the Environment from British Columbia supported a full public hearing of the Alcan project which we have talked about in the House before. That is another example of the considerable debate around fish habitat and the need to ensure that we have the enforcement and compliance in the law by the fisheries officers carrying out the rules and regulations that we pass in this House.
This provision for an annual report is an important one, and I am glad to see that the House will be supporting it.

Mr. Speaker, I would just put on the record that if you overfish and you catch fish that you are not licensed to catch, you will be convicted unless you do it on a foreign boat in Canadian waters.
Not only that, but what is happening off our coast is that, if a foreign nation catches more than it is legally allowed to catch, the observer comes in two weeks hence, reports it, and the ship is then moved either north, south, east or west. They do not have to throw away the incidental catch or the catch which is in excess of the buy catch. Shame! Shame on the Government of Canada.
The Canadian will come in and he will be arrested. But, if you have a good lawyer, Mr. Speaker, here is a great clause in the bill. "No person shall be convicted of an offence under the act if the person establishes that the person (a) exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of an offence or (b) reasonably and honestly believed"-and the Minister of Justice should be overjoyed with this one-"in the existence of facts that if true would render the person's conduct innocent."
December 5, 1990

That is pretty clear, is it not? You get a big lawyer. You have to have the money to pay for your lawyer, like the Government of Canada thinks most people have. It will cost you a lot of dough. No problem getting over this act. But the poor fisherman who is brought in, who is supposed to be represented by members of Parliament, will get it right between the teeth with this legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 24
(a)	by striking out, in the English version, line 24 at page 18 and
substituting the following therefor:
"control of fisheries or fish habitat or the";
(b)	by striking out lines 33 to 48 at page 18 and substituting the
following:
"(h) directing the person to submit to the Minister, on application by the Minister within three years after the date of the conviction, any information respecting the activities of the person that the court considers appropriate in the circumstances; and
(i) requiring the person to comply with any other conditions that the court considers appropriate for securing the person's good conduct and for preventing the person from repeating the offence or committing other offences under this Act."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on Motion No. 4, this particular amendment to Bill C-74, and to comment about how soon we will be debating at third reading this legislation. The amendment is going to require a person convicted, if the court so orders, to pay for promoting the proper management and control of fisheries or fish habitat.
When the bill first came to committee it just talked about fish. We have included fish habitat in this amendment, and the government is supporting it. That is particularly important, given all the concerns we have in terms of protecting our creeks and rivers from logging
Government Orders
operations, pulp mill pollution and others and of ensuring that more than just a balance among our resource industries happen and that we are successful in extracting our resources in a sustainable way which not only protects the environment but ensures that the resources will continue in perpetuity for all of us to benefit from.
An interesting aspect of this amendment is the fact that we are not only talking about paying for the damage, which I find very difficult to accept as a principle. It is like having people take over your house for the weekend and they wreck the place, and then when you come back on Sunday night they say: "That is okay. We will pay for it". That is not the way to go about inviting any of your friends or guests over, if they are still friends. Nor is it any way to allow the destruction of our fish habitat.
This amendment goes beyond asking people to fess up and to provide some dollars. Witnesses said to us in committee that it would be just a cost of doing business, that it was going to be another couple of hundred dollars and on we go; there was no change. This amendment will ensure that damages are paid from what the courts order. It will also ensure that there is emphasis on the fisheries officers being out there and that they have confidence that their department realizes the importance of the rules and regulations they are policing. As well it will ensure that anyone convicted of a crime will understand how important that is and that they will participate in helping to promote the protection and enhancement of our fish habitat.
It is a positive amendment. It is moving in the right direction, and I hope the House will support it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this amendment was accepted in committee. I think it is important to put on record that there were some minor legal changes, some wording changes which my friend opposite has reintroduced. The government supports this amendment and thinks it is a good step as well.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a brief comment. It is fine and dandy to talk about fish habitat. It is fine and dandy to talk about fines. It is fine and dandy to have such glorious words about protecting the fishing environment and the fishing habitat.

Government Orders
However, 135 gigantic, monstrous vessels from nine foreign nations are raking the grounds around the coast of Canada, while we sit in this Chamber and figure out what fines to put on Canadian fishermen who might be violating the fish habitat of Canada.
A lot of things have to change in this country, and that is one of them. Canadians vessels are not allowed to go into the waters or any one of those countries; not one of those countries. It is not allowed. There would be a war. We would be chased out. They are in our waters with all of this gigantic gear, all computerized, raking all of the grounds on the continental shelf, ignored by the Government of Canada. In fact, the numbers are going up every year. No wonder the fishing resource is destroyed together with the fishing habitat.
